```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#",
                  fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.5)
library(Rfast)
library(mixsqp)
library(ggplot2)
for (f in list.files("/sc/arion/projects/ad-omics/haochen/rss_qc/susieR/R/",
                     full.names = TRUE, pattern = "\\.R$")) source(f)
library(crayon)
```

`susie_rss` fine-maps a region from summary statistics z-scores and an LD
matrix. When the LD matrix does not match the summary statistics, the fit
can report extra, spurious credible sets (CSs). This vignette walks through
the workflow we recommend for handling this, step by step, on simulated
data:

0. **Align alleles first.** Before any statistical check, make sure the
   summary statistics and the LD reference use the same variants and the
   same effect alleles.
1. **Check allele coding with kriging.** Sign errors in the
   z-scores (allele flips) show up as outliers. Fix them before
   fine-mapping. The kriging diagnostic is covered in detail in the
   [RSS diagnostic vignette](https://stephenslab.github.io/susieR/articles/susierss_diagnostic.html).
2. **Fit with SuSiE-rRSS.** SuSiE-rRSS (robust RSS) is SuSiE-RSS made
   robust to an LD reference that does not exactly match the summary
   statistics. It is run through `susie_rss` function by setting `R_finite = B` and
   `R_mismatch = "eb_mix"`, where `B` is the sample size of your LD
   reference panel. This accounts for an LD matrix estimated from an
   external reference panel, drawn from a population that can differ from
   the summary statistics population.
3. **Check `SER_fallback`.** If it is `TRUE`, the corrected fit is still not
   reliable; report the one-effect (SER) model instead.
4. **With several reference panels, pass them all.** For meta-analysis
   summary statistics, give `susie_rss` a **list** of reference panels. It
   estimates how much weight each panel gets, then fine-maps with the
   weighted (mixed) LD.

## Load the package and data

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(susieR)
data(rss_mismatch_cases, package = "susieR")
if (!exists("rss_mismatch_cases"))
  load(file.path("..", "data", "rss_mismatch_cases.RData"))
cases <- rss_mismatch_cases
```

## Case design

All examples are simulated summary statistics for regions with one causal
variant. The first four cases simulate a phenotype from GTEx genotypes
(n = 838). The multi-panel case simulates phenotypes for an
African-ancestry cohort and a European-ancestry cohort and meta-analyzes
them.

| Case | Step | Summary statistics | LD reference | Issue |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `allele_flip` | 1 | GTEx, n = 838 | in-sample GTEx LD | 1% of the variants have the sign of their z-score reversed (2 in this region) |
| `ld_mismatch` | 2 | GTEx, n = 838 | 1000 Genomes EUR LD, B = 489 | external LD panel |
| `ld_mismatch_sketch` | 2 | GTEx, n = 838 | ADSP sketch, B = 500 | external LD panel, given as a genotype sketch instead of an LD matrix |
| `ser_fallback` | 3 | GTEx, n = 838 | 1000 Genomes EUR LD, B = 489 | external LD panel |
| `multi_panel` | 4 | 1000 Genomes AFR (n = 400) + UK Biobank unrelated EUR (n = 400), total n = 800 | AFR and EUR panel LD | no single panel matches the mixed summary statistics |

## Data

The inputs for all five cases are packed in one list. Each element holds
what `susie_rss` needs:

- `z`: the summary statistics z-scores;
- `R`: the LD matrix (a named list of LD matrices for `multi_panel`), or
  `X`: a factor matrix (genotype sketch) of the reference panel, used
  instead of `R`;
- `n`: the summary statistics sample size;
- `B`: the reference panel sample size, used as `R_finite`.

Because the data are simulated, each element also stores `causal`, the
index of the true causal variant. The external-reference cases also store
`z_insample` and `R_insample`: the z-scores and the in-sample LD on the
same variants. `allele_flip` stores `z_clean` (the z-scores before
flipping) and `flip_id` (the indices of the flipped variants);
`multi_panel` stores `prop`, the true proportion of summary statistics
samples from each ancestry.

A few small helpers for the comparisons below. `fit_table()` puts several
fits side by side, including how many CSs contain the causal variant;
`cs_summary()` lists the CSs of one fit; `plot_region()` draws PIPs only in
the part of the region around the CSs and the causal variant.

```{r helpers}
truth <- function(x) {
  b <- numeric(length(x$z))
  b[x$causal] <- 1
  b
}

cs_summary <- function(fit, causal = NULL) {
  cs <- fit$sets$cs
  if (length(cs) == 0) return(data.frame(note = "no credible sets"))
  data.frame(
    cs          = names(cs),
    size        = lengths(cs),
    purity      = fit$sets$purity$min.abs.corr,
    top_variant = vapply(cs, function(v) v[which.max(fit$pip[v])], numeric(1)),
    max_pip     = vapply(cs, function(v) max(fit$pip[v]), numeric(1)),
    has_causal  = if (is.null(causal)) NA else
                    vapply(cs, function(v) any(v %in% causal), logical(1)),
    row.names = NULL
  )
}

diag_value <- function(fit, name) {
  d <- fit$R_finite_diagnostics
  if (is.null(d) || is.null(d[[name]])) NA else d[[name]][1]
}

fit_row <- function(fit, causal = NULL) {
  if (is.null(fit))
    return(data.frame(n_cs = NA, n_cs_with_causal = NA, converged = NA,
                      Q_art = NA, R_sensitivity_flag = NA, SER_fallback = NA))
  cs <- fit$sets$cs
  data.frame(
    n_cs = length(cs),
    n_cs_with_causal = if (is.null(causal)) NA else
      sum(vapply(cs, function(v) any(v %in% causal), logical(1))),
    converged = if (is.null(fit$converged)) NA else as.logical(fit$converged),
    Q_art = as.numeric(diag_value(fit, "Q_art")),
    R_sensitivity_flag = as.logical(diag_value(fit, "R_sensitivity_flag")),
    SER_fallback = as.logical(diag_value(fit, "SER_fallback"))
  )
}

fit_table <- function(fits, causal = NULL) {
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, fit_row, causal = causal))
  out <- data.frame(method = names(fits), out, row.names = NULL)
  out[, colSums(!is.na(out)) > 0, drop = FALSE]
}

kriging_outliers <- function(kr) {
  which(kr$conditional_dist$logLR > 2 & abs(kr$conditional_dist$z) > 2)
}

plot_region <- function(fit, x, main, pad = 30) {
  idx <- c(unlist(fit$sets$cs), x$causal)
  if (length(idx) == 0) idx <- which.max(fit$pip)
  pos <- max(1, min(idx) - pad):min(length(fit$pip), max(idx) + pad)
  susie_plot(fit, y = "PIP", b = truth(x), pos = pos, add_legend = TRUE,
             main = main)
}
```

## Step 1: find allele flips with kriging

In this region the LD matrix is in-sample: it was computed from the same
838 GTEx individuals as the summary statistics. The sign of the z-score was
then reversed at 1% of the variants, as happens when the effect allele is
coded differently in the summary statistics and the LD reference. Since the
LD itself is correct, any problem here comes from allele flips.

Before running kriging, we strongly encourage checking allele consistency
between the summary statistics and the LD reference, for example with
[pecotmr](https://statfungen.github.io/pecotmr/articles/rss-qc.html). If the
inconsistency is widespread, for example because of different variant
naming systems, statistical methods can fail arbitrarily badly. Kriging is
a check for any flipped variants left over after that QC.

### Kriging check

The kriging diagnostic predicts each z-score from all the others using the
LD matrix. A variant whose observed z-score has the opposite sign of its
prediction is flagged as a likely allele flip and drawn in red. See the
[RSS diagnostic vignette](https://stephenslab.github.io/susieR/articles/susierss_diagnostic.html)
for details.

```{r kriging-flip}
af <- cases$allele_flip
kr_flip <- kriging_rss(af$z, af$R, n = af$n)
kr_flip$plot
out_flip <- kriging_outliers(kr_flip)
c(flagged = length(out_flip),
  truly_flipped = sum(out_flip %in% af$flip_id),
  total_flipped = length(af$flip_id))
```

Kriging flags 1 variant, and it is a true flip. The other flip is at a
variant with a small z-score, where a sign error changes little, so it
matters much less for fine-mapping.

For reference, the same check on the unflipped z-scores, with the same
in-sample LD, flags no variants:

```{r kriging-clean}
kr_clean <- kriging_rss(af$z_clean, af$R, n = af$n)
kr_clean$plot
length(kriging_outliers(kr_clean))
```

### Fine-mapping before and after the correction

We reverse the sign of the flagged variant and fine-map with the
original, flipped and corrected z-scores.

```{r fit-flip}

z_fix <- af$z
z_fix[out_flip] <- -z_fix[out_flip]

fit_flip  <- susie_rss(z = af$z, R = af$R, n = af$n)
fit_fix   <- susie_rss(z = z_fix, R = af$R, n = af$n)
fit_clean <- susie_rss(z = af$z_clean, R = af$R, n = af$n)
knitr::kable(fit_table(list(original = fit_clean,
                            flipped = fit_flip,
                            kriging_corrected = fit_fix),
                       causal = af$causal), digits = 3)
```

With the flipped z-scores, `susie_rss` reports 5 CSs, none containing the
causal variant, and does not converge. After the correction it reports 1 CS
containing the causal variant, the same as with the original z-scores.

```{r plot-flip}
plot_region(fit_clean, af, main = "original z-scores")
if (!is.null(fit_flip))
  plot_region(fit_flip, af, main = "flipped z-scores")
plot_region(fit_fix, af, main = "after kriging correction")
```

## Step 2: reference panel mismatch

In this case the alleles are aligned, but the LD matrix comes from an
external panel (489 Europeans from 1000 Genomes), rather than from the 838
GTEx individuals in the summary statistics. GTEx samples are of mixed
ancestry, so this LD differs from the LD of the summary statistics samples.
Running kriging first finds nothing to correct:

```{r kriging-lm}
lm <- cases$ld_mismatch
kr_lm <- kriging_rss(lm$z, lm$R, n = lm$n)
kr_lm$plot
length(kriging_outliers(kr_lm))
```

However, fine-mapping with the external reference is still misled:

```{r fit-lm}
fit_in <- susie_rss(z = lm$z_insample, R = lm$R_insample, n = lm$n)
fit_lm <- susie_rss(z = lm$z, R = lm$R, n = lm$n)
knitr::kable(fit_table(list(in_sample_LD = fit_in, ordinary = fit_lm),
                       causal = lm$causal), digits = 3)
```

With the 1000 Genomes LD, ordinary `susie_rss` reports 2 CSs, only one of which contains the causal variant. With
the in-sample LD there is a single CS.

### SuSiE-rRSS: `R_finite` and `R_mismatch`

SuSiE-rRSS accounts for this with two options of `susie_rss`:

- `R_finite = B` tells `susie_rss` that the LD was estimated from `B`
  reference individuals, here 489, and inflates the uncertainty of each
  update accordingly.
- `R_mismatch = "eb_mix"` estimates from the data on how much additional LD
  mismatch the region has. It then applies that extra
  uncertainty to each variant in proportion to how likely the variant's
  residual is to be mismatch rather than true signal.

```{r fit-lm-eb}
fit_lm_rrss <- susie_rss(z = lm$z, R = lm$R, n = lm$n,
                       R_finite = lm$B, R_mismatch = "eb_mix")
knitr::kable(fit_table(list(in_sample_LD = fit_in, ordinary = fit_lm,
                            `SuSiE-rRSS` = fit_lm_rrss),
                       causal = lm$causal), digits = 3)
```

With SuSiE-rRSS (`R_finite = 489`, `R_mismatch = "eb_mix"`), the fit reports 1 CS and drops the spurious second CS of the ordinary fit.
`SER_fallback` (explained in Step 3) is `FALSE`, so the SuSiE-rRSS fit is the
result to report.

```{r plot-lm}
plot_region(fit_in, lm, main = "in-sample LD")
plot_region(fit_lm, lm, main = "1000 Genomes LD, ordinary")
plot_region(fit_lm_rrss, lm, main = "1000 Genomes LD, SuSiE-rRSS")
```

### The same with a sketch of the reference panel

Instead of a LD matrix, the reference panel can be given as a factor
matrix (sketch) `X` with p columns (p = number of variants). The workflow is
unchanged: pass `X` instead of `R`.

Here the reference is a sketch of the ADSP panel with 500 rows:

```{r kriging-sk}
sk <- cases$ld_mismatch_sketch
kr_sk <- kriging_rss(sk$z, cor(sk$X), n = sk$n)
kr_sk$plot
length(kriging_outliers(kr_sk))
```

Kriging again flags nothing. For a sketch, `R_finite` is the sketch
dimension, the number of rows of `X`, here 500.

```{r fit-sk}
fit_sk_in <- susie_rss(z = sk$z_insample, R = sk$R_insample, n = sk$n)
fit_sk    <- susie_rss(z = sk$z, X = sk$X, n = sk$n)
fit_sk_rrss <- susie_rss(z = sk$z, X = sk$X, n = sk$n,
                       R_finite = sk$B, R_mismatch = "eb_mix")
knitr::kable(fit_table(list(in_sample_LD = fit_sk_in, ordinary = fit_sk,
                            `SuSiE-rRSS` = fit_sk_rrss),
                       causal = sk$causal), digits = 3)
```

With the sketch, ordinary `susie_rss` reports 4 CSs and does not converge.
With SuSiE-rRSS (`R_finite = 500`, `R_mismatch = "eb_mix"`), it reports
1 CS with a single variant, and `SER_fallback` is `FALSE`.

```{r plot-sk}
plot_region(fit_sk, sk, main = "ADSP sketch, ordinary")
plot_region(fit_sk_rrss, sk, main = "ADSP sketch, SuSiE-rRSS")
```

## Step 3: when SuSiE-rRSS is not enough, `SER_fallback` points to the SER model

This region uses the same 1000 Genomes reference (B = 489) on another
simulated dataset. As before, start with kriging:

```{r kriging-sf}
sf <- cases$ser_fallback
kr_sf <- kriging_rss(sf$z, sf$R, n = sf$n)
kr_sf$plot
length(kriging_outliers(kr_sf))
```

Kriging flags nothing, so we fit `susie_rss` with the in-sample LD, the
1000 Genomes LD, and the 1000 Genomes LD with SuSiE-rRSS:

```{r fit-sf}
fit_sf_in <- susie_rss(z = sf$z_insample, R = sf$R_insample, n = sf$n)
fit_sf    <- susie_rss(z = sf$z, R = sf$R, n = sf$n)
fit_sf_rrss <- susie_rss(z = sf$z, R = sf$R, n = sf$n,
                       R_finite = sf$B, R_mismatch = "eb_mix")
knitr::kable(fit_table(list(in_sample_LD = fit_sf_in, ordinary = fit_sf,
                            `SuSiE-rRSS` = fit_sf_rrss),
                       causal = sf$causal), digits = 3)
```

The ordinary fit reports 4 CSs, none containing the causal variant, and
does not converge. The SuSiE-rRSS fit does not converge either and still
reports 4 CSs, none of which contain the causal variant. `susie_rss` prints a warning that
the result may be unreliable: `SER_fallback` is `TRUE`.

### What `SER_fallback` checks

`SER_fallback` is `TRUE` when **either** of two checks fails:

- **Residual check** (`artifact_flag`): `Q_art` is the share of the fitted
  residual that lies in directions the LD matrix barely supports. A value
  above 0.1 means part of the residual cannot be explained by the LD.
- **Sensitivity check** (`R_sensitivity_flag`): for each CS, how much its
  log Bayes factor drops once LD uncertainty is accounted for. A drop above
  30 means the CS depends on uncertain LD subtraction, which is how
  imperfect conditioning creates spurious signals.

```{r bf-attenuation}
round(fit_sf_rrss$R_finite_diagnostics$bf_attenuation$cs_max, 2)
```

`Q_art` is 0.082, below 0.1, so the residual check passes. But every CS
loses far more than 30 in log Bayes factor (from 467 to 1199), so the
sensitivity check fails.

### The SER model

When `SER_fallback` is `TRUE`, the fit provides a one-effect model in
`fit$R_finite_diagnostics$ser_model`. It is a single-effect regression
(SER), as in Maller et al. (2012): it assumes one causal variant in the
region, so it cannot report extra CSs created by LD mismatch. Its PIPs are
the single row of `alpha`. Using the SER model helps avoid false
discoveries.

```{r plot-ser}
ser <- fit_sf_rrss$R_finite_diagnostics$ser_model
plot_region(ser, sf, main = "SER model")
```

Conclusion: report the full fit from step 2 unless `SER_fallback` is `TRUE`, in which case report
the SER model.

```{r final-fit}
final_fit <- function(fit) {
  if (isTRUE(fit$R_finite_diagnostics$SER_fallback))
    fit$R_finite_diagnostics$ser_model
  else fit
}
knitr::kable(fit_table(list(in_sample_LD = fit_sf_in, ordinary = fit_sf,
                            `SuSiE-rRSS` = fit_sf_rrss,
                            SER_model = final_fit(fit_sf_rrss)),
                       causal = sf$causal), digits = 3)
```

The SER model reports 1 CS of 3 variants, which contains the causal
variant, with a top PIP of 0.33.

## Step 4: several reference panels

These summary statistics are a meta-analysis of an African-ancestry cohort
(400 samples) and a European-ancestry cohort of unrelated UK Biobank
samples (400 samples), so each ancestry makes up 50% of the 800 samples.
Neither the AFR nor the EUR reference panel alone matches the LD of this
mixed sample.

Pass both panels as a named list. `susie_rss` then works in two stages:

1. It estimates the weight `omega` of each panel, so that the mixed LD
   `omega_AFR * R_AFR + omega_EUR * R_EUR` best fits the z-scores.
2. It fine-maps with that mixed LD.

```{r fit-mp}
mp <- cases$multi_panel
fit_mp <- susie_rss(z = mp$z, R = mp$R, n = mp$n)
knitr::kable(data.frame(panel = names(mp$R),
                        estimated_weight = fit_mp$omega_weights,
                        true_proportion = mp$prop,
                        row.names = NULL), digits = 3)
knitr::kable(cs_summary(fit_mp, mp$causal), digits = 3)
```

The estimated weights, 0.409 for AFR and 0.591 for EUR, are close to the
true proportions of 0.5 and 0.5. The fit reports 1 CS: a single variant,
which is the causal variant.

For comparison, the fit also keeps one fit per panel, which is used to
choose where the weight estimation starts:

```{r single-panel}
spf <- fit_mp$single_panel_fits
names(spf) <- paste0(names(mp$R), "_only")
knitr::kable(fit_table(c(spf, list(mixed = fit_mp)), causal = mp$causal),
             digits = 3)
```

With a single panel, the fit reports extra CSs: 5 with the AFR panel and 3
with the EUR panel (which does not converge), and in each case only one of
them contains the causal variant. With the mixed LD there is a single CS,
the causal variant.

If the panels are given as factor matrices instead of LD matrices, pass
`X = list(AFR = X_AFR, EUR = X_EUR)`.

## Summary

For fine-mapping with summary statistics and external LD:

- **Align alleles first, before any statistical check.** Make sure the
  summary statistics and the LD reference use the same genome build and the
  same variants, for example with
  `pecotmr::summaryStatsQc()`. 
- **Then check with kriging.** Red outliers point to allele flips left over
  after the QC. Fix them, then confirm with kriging that they are gone.
- **Fit with SuSiE-rRSS** (`susie_rss` with `R_finite` and
  `R_mismatch = "eb_mix"`) when the LD comes from a reference panel, given
  either as an LD matrix `R` or as a genotype sketch `X`.
- **Check `fit$R_finite_diagnostics$SER_fallback`.** If it is `TRUE`, report
  `fit$R_finite_diagnostics$ser_model` instead of the full fit.
- **With several reference panels, pass them as a list.** `susie_rss`
  estimates the panel weights (`fit$omega_weights`) and fine-maps with the
  mixed LD. This can be combined with `R_finite` and `R_mismatch` as above.
